newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. ships Iraqi missile parts to U.S.
newsitem.headline: U.N. ships Iraqi missile parts to U.S.

text.p: The United Nations has sent the scrapped components of banned Iraqi missiles for analysis in the United States, a U.N. arms official in Baghdad said on Saturday.

"The remnants of the missile engines that have been stored in Baghdad and at Shomoukh site in its outskirts have been removed to Bahrain on their way to the United States for examination," Roger Knight, deputy-director of the Baghdad Ongoing Monitoring Verification Centre, told Reuters.
Knight said the parts were sent on Friday in two separate flights from Habaniya airport, 60 km (38 miles) west of Baghdad to Bahrain.
Iraq and the United Nations agreed late last month to have the scrapped missile engines analysed abroad to see whether they were imported from the former Soviet Union or locally produced.
The engines, about 100, were packed in boxes and kept under U.N. surveillance at Baghdad and at Shomoukh, a missile site on the outskirts of the Iraqi capital.
Most of them were excavated last year but Iraq refused to send them to the United States, favouring France or Russia. They were unilaterally destroyed by Iraq in 1992.
Iraq's approval to have them shipped abroad came following a visit to Baghdad last month by Rolf Ekeus, chairman of the U.N. Special Commission on Iraq.

Under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire Iraq is banned from keeping or manufacturing missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles). Ekeus says he still cannot ascertain that Baghdad does not keep any such missiles.
Ekeus must certify Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations will lift curbs on Iraqi oil exports, although Baghdad is allowed limited oil exports under a humanitarian deal.
